labels.faithful: every claim is supported by the retrieved passages and the answer addresses the question
labels.unsupported: at least one claim is not in the retrieved passages, including true facts from the model's own knowledge
labels.non-answer: declines, or says the passages do not cover the question

answerable.question: How much does ngrok cost if I want an SSH port that stays the same after my GPU server reboots?

support.quote: An A100 has about 80 GB of HBM with a bandwidth of ~2 TB/s.
A A100 has about ~20 MB total (spread across 108 SMs) with ~19 TB/s bandwidth. This is roughly **10x** the bandwidth of HBM but nearly **4000x** smaller in capacity.

answerable.question: Why did he switch to per-token loss normalization when training SFT?
answerable.reference: With sequence-level normalization, longer sequences contributed more to the gradient than short ones, which made gradient updates high variance and unstable. Normalizing by the number of response tokens made the gradients much more stable and slightly improved accuracy.

support.quote: with variable-length sequences (my training examples ranged from short to quite long), longer sequences contribute more to the gradient than shorter ones. This creates high variance in gradient updates.
The difference was noticeable with subtle improved accuracy. More importantly, the gradients became much more stable with per-token normalization.

answerable.question: Why is FlashAttention's backward pass faster even though it recomputes the attention matrix?
answerable.reference: Attention is memory-bound, so the extra compute costs little, while not storing the N by N probability matrix removes the large HBM reads and writes that dominate standard attention.

support.quote: In practice, FlashAttention backward pass is *faster* than standard attention despite doing more FLOPs, because it eliminates the massive HBM reads and writes of $P$ (remember FlashAttention is memory-bound!).
This trades memory for compute. Since, standard attention is memory-bound, the additional compute is small in comparison.

answerable.question: How does DPO get away without a reward model or reinforcement learning?
answerable.reference: DPO optimizes the same KL-constrained objective as PPO-based RLHF but turns it into a single supervised classification loss on preference pairs. Because the Bradley-Terry model depends only on reward differences, the intractable partition function cancels, so no sampling, value function or clipping is needed.

support.quote: The key insight is that DPO implicitly optimizes the **same** objective as PPO-based RLHF (reward maximization with a KL-divergence constraint) but it replaces the entire reward model + PPO loop with a single supervised objective on preference pairs. There is no sampling during training, no value function, no clipping, just a classification loss!

The derivation hinges on one observation that the Bradley-Terry model only cares about reward differences and this causes the intractable partition function from analytical solution to cancel out completely.

answerable.question: How did he fit GRPO training on a single 24 GB RTX 4090?
answerable.reference: He tracked peak memory and used gradient checkpointing, vLLM sleep mode to offload vLLM's KV cache and weights to CPU while training, and the 8-bit AdamW optimizer, with a microbatch size of 1 and gradient accumulation.

support.quote: The simplest one is to enable gradient checkpointing which recomputes activations during backward pass instead of storing them.
This is quite a nice trick to offload vLLM KV cache and weights to CPU during the training phase (when vLLM is not generating).
I added an option to use bitsandbytes `AdamW8bit` optimizer instead of the default `AdamW` optimizer.
After all the above optimization tricks, I was able to successfully train with `rollout_batch_size=256`, `group_size=8`, `gradient_accumulation_steps=256` (microbatch size = 1) on 24 GB.

answerable.question: Why can Qwen3.5-27B run with a 64K context on a 24 GB card?
answerable.reference: Qwen3.5 is a hybrid model: only every fourth layer uses standard attention and the rest use Gated DeltaNet with a fixed-size state, so its KV cache is far smaller than a pure transformer's.

support.quote: Qwen3.5 uses a Gated DeltaNet + Gated Attention hybrid architecture. Only every 4th layer has standard attention (16 out of 64 for 27B) and the rest use DeltaNet which maintains a fixed-size state regardless of context length. This makes the KV cache dramatically smaller than a pure transformer of the same size which is why 64K context fits on a 24 GB card at all.

answerable.question: Why does he run the GPT plus local GLM setup in OpenCode instead of Claude Code or Codex?
answerable.reference: Claude Code and Codex subagents cannot point at a different endpoint: Codex still sends a subagent's requests to OpenAI, so his GLM subagent failed, and Claude Code subagents can change model but not endpoint. In OpenCode every agent or subagent can use a model from a different provider.

support.quote: Codex picks up the role but still sends its requests to OpenAI so the subagent fails right away
Claude Code has the same limitation: a subagent can pick a different model but not a different endpoint
every agent or subagent can have its own model from a different provider which is the one most important feature this setup needs

answerable.question: What does the Kalman gain do when the sensor is unreliable?
answerable.reference: When measurement noise is large the gain shrinks toward zero, so the filter mostly trusts its own prediction rather than the measurement.

support.quote: When the measurement noise $R$ is large (an unreliable sensor), $K_k$ shrinks toward zero and the filter mostly trusts its own prediction.

answerable.question: How was spectral clustering changed to handle overlapping speakers in the SLT 2021 diarization work?
answerable.reference: An overlap detector feeds a modified version of scikit-learn's spectral clustering: the discretize step takes an extra overlap vector and uses it to give overlapping segments a second speaker label.

support.quote: The code consists of two parts: overlap detector, and our modified spectral clustering method for overlap-aware diarization.
We have implemented the diarization recipe in Kaldi, and modified scikit-learn's spectral clustering class for our modification.
by adding an additional argument which specifies the overlap vector. The vector is used in L141-148 to assign a second label to the overlapping segments.

answerable.question: What deep learning work has Aayush done on seismic data?
answerable.reference: At Shell he built denoising models for seismic data, uncertainty quantification for subsurface imaging and learned Hessian operators for wave-equation optimization. At TU Delft he used deep learning super-resolution (SRCNN, EDSR, VDSR) to upscale seismic data 2x in the spatial direction and remove spatial aliasing, published in 2019 in First Break.

support.quote: Applied deep learning across Shell's seismic research: denoising models for seismic data, uncertainty quantification for subsurface imaging, and learned Hessian operators for wave-equation optimization.

I used deep learning super-resolution (SRCNN, EDSR, VDSR) to upscale seismic data by 2x in the spatial direction and remove spatial aliasing. This work was published as a paper back in 2019, built during my time at TU Delft and University of Amsterdam.
Spatial aliasing removal using deep learning super-resolution
[First Break, 37(9), 87-92]

answerable.question: Did fine-tuning a small open model beat GPT-4o on the ViGGO extraction task?
answerable.reference: Partly. GPT-4o with few-shot prompting got an exact match on only about 30% of examples. A Llama-3-8B fine-tuned on at most 1,000 examples, after a clearer prompt template, surpassed GPT-4o on exact match and function name match, but did not match GPT-4 and Claude 3.5 Sonnet on every metric.

support.quote: The best the model can do is to provide the exact match only for **30%** of the examples.
I will use a maximum of 1000 examples for fine-tuning any LLM model
Notably, the model now surpasses GPT-4o's scores for `exact_match` and `function_name_match`.
Although the fine-tuned llama-3-8b model doesn't match the performance of GPT-4 and Sonnet 3.5 on all metrics.

answerable.question: How does time-series data come into Aayush's current job, and where does the Kalman filter fit?
answerable.reference: At Applied Computing he deploys AI for live process plants, which includes monitoring the time-series models they deploy, and time-series data is an important part of that work. He uses the Kalman filter mainly as a preprocessing tool (denoising, decomposition, gap filling), while actual predictions come from ML-based forecasting models.

support.quote: Behind that sit ever-improving evals, monitoring for the time-series models we deploy, a reasoning layer that explains each recommendation to operators
An important part of my current work involves time-series data.
Most of the value I get from the Kalman filter has nothing to do with using it as the final forecasting model. It is a pre-processing workhorse
For actual predictions we anyway rely on ML-based forecasting models.

answerable.question: How has he used vLLM inside his own training runs?
answerable.reference: For SFT he ran vLLM colocated on the training GPU for fast intermediate evaluation. For GRPO he reused that colocate setup to run training, evaluation and rollout generation on one GPU, and turned on vLLM sleep mode to offload its KV cache and weights to CPU during the training phase.

support.quote: I wanted to run intermediate evaluations during training using vLLM for fast inference.
I switched to the `colocate` approach, running vLLM on the same device as the training model.
I used the same vLLM colocate setup and workarounds as I did for SFT
This allowed me to run the training loop and intermediate evaluations and rollout generations on a single GPU.
This is quite a nice trick to offload vLLM KV cache and weights to CPU during the training phase (when vLLM is not generating).
